newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Minister says Russians face mass poverty.
newsitem.headline: Minister says Russians face mass poverty.

text.p: Russia's social policy chief said on Monday a quarter of Russians were living below subsistence levels and complained he had little power or money to put things right.

First Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Ilyushin, in overall charge of social policy, said real incomes had plunged 40 percent since the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991, unemployment had risen and many regions faced acute social problems.

"However deplorable it is, we have to acknowledge that mass poverty has arisen and the number of citizens with incomes below the subsistence minimum is a quarter of the whole population of Russia," Ilyushin told a news conference.

"The main and strongest impression that I have taken from two months of work is that I can resolve practically nothing. I do not have that part of the budget and financial resources with which I can take decisions," he said.

President Boris Yeltsin, re-elected for a second term in July, has pledged there will be no turning back on the tough pro-market reforms underway since 1992. But he has ordered ministers to give higher priority to social reform and raising the living standards of ordinary Russians.

The discreetly veiled gap between Soviet-era rich and poor has turned into a broad abd very evident chasm in the new Russia, where an elite has amassed vast fortunes and sky-high inflation of the early years of reform has beggared millions.

At the same time, the economy is undergoing a severe payments crisis. Companies do not pay suppliers or workers for months and huge tax arrears build up, restricting the government's ability to tackle social problems.
Ilyushin, who moved from Yeltsin's administration to join the government, said money for social programmes was not always going to the right people.
"Sponging has increased and there are limited possibilities of getting help to those who really need it," he said.
He said industrial production had fallen four percent in the first half of this year, but unemployment had risen only 1.5 percent.
"The fall in production and worsening in the financial situation of companies has not been accompanied by a corresponding reduction in the numbers in work," Ilyushin said.
Thousands of Russian companies have been hit hard by the loss of Soviet-era markets and exposure to foreign competition. But bankruptcy and redundancies are rare.
"If 10 years ago, the word unemployment made our hair stand on end, today we first have to ask what kind of unemployment and what level there should be or can be in Russia," Ilyushin said.

The communist opposition, which emerged as the strongest performer in December's parliamentary election by playing on the hardships caused by reform, says the government's 1997 draft budget does not provide enough for social needs.
Parliament rejected the first reading of the budget last week and will meet again on Wednesday to decide what to do.
Ilyushin said education had received just 65 percent of the money allocated to it in the 1996 budget, health care 60 percent and culture 30 percent.
A state committee on social reform has drawn up a draft social reform programme which seeks to raise living standards, rationalise the labour market and improve infrastructure.
The aim of the first two years (1996-7) is to stabilise living standards, gradually reduce poverty and stop mass unemployment.
In the second phase (1998-2000), the programme, which is still under discussion, says conditions will be created for real growth in incomes and for poverty to be rooted out.
